metadata.title: Transport, Do Not Repair
metadata.note: cli-explainer spine, weekly work report, claude-hai channel. Sequel to last week: that ledger closed with 'gate 2 cannot clear'; this commit closes it. Built to the PROOF rubric — FRAMEWORK (three questions for any pipeline stage: DECIDES / REFUSES / EVIDENCE) shown as a structure before any example, both steps scored on it, and a falsifiability beat the framework PREDICTS (axis 3 — the CRLF bug made the evidence platform-dependent). Title is taken verbatim from the ingest script's own load-bearing rule. Every number verified against a live run — see SOURCES.md / FACTCHECK.md.

beats.role_note: COLD OPEN LAW — composer, ask lands answered. Speaks the author's name. HAI short-form greeting.
beats.narration_text: I'm Uday Sonawane, and this is my week on Mycroft. Two more pipeline steps are written. The interesting part is what they refuse to do.
beats.new_visual_element: Claude composer, the week's ask, answered

shot.show: the Claude composer with the week's ask and its three-line answer

props.command: claude "write steps 2 and 3 of the market-sentiment recipe against the frozen corpus"
props.segment: Uday Sonawane · Transport, Do Not Repair

beats.role_note: continuity with last episode's ledger — kept tight so the FRAMEWORK lands inside the first ~20s
beats.narration_text: Last week ended with a ledger. Five steps unwritten. No run envelope, so gate two could not clear. This week two of those steps exist: ingest, and shape validation. Writing them raised a question I did not expect.
beats.new_visual_element: last week's open ledger, two rows closing

shot.show: last episode's STILL OPEN list with two items resolving to done
shot.visual_intent: Last week's four open rows appear in terracotta. Two of them — run-envelope absent, gate 2 cannot clear — resolve to ink and gain a check. The remaining two stay terracotta. The ledger is the through-line between episodes.

beats.role_note: PROOF rubric — the reusable three questions, shown AS A STRUCTURE before either step is examined
beats.narration_text: Here it is, as three questions you can ask of any pipeline stage. One: what does this stage decide? Two: what must it refuse to decide, even though it easily could? Three: what evidence does it leave that someone else can re-check? Most pipeline bugs I have written came from getting question two wrong. A stage doing a little more than its job.
beats.new_visual_element: the three questions, as a numbered structure

shot.show: three numbered cards: DECIDES / REFUSES / EVIDENCE, each with its question
shot.visual_intent: Three cards land in a row, one per narration step: DECIDES (what it judges), REFUSES (what it must not judge, though it could), EVIDENCE (what a reviewer can re-check). They stay on screen as the rubric both steps are scored against.

beats.role_note: cycle 1 ask — SPARK-LINE LAW: greeting is the spark line
beats.narration_text: So, step two. Ingest. Move the declared sources into the raw layer. And the temptation is right there: to be helpful, to fix what you can plainly see is broken on the way past.

shot.show: the Claude composer carrying the step-2 prompt

props.command: claude "write step 2: ingest the declared sources into data/raw/ — and do not repair anything on the way"
output: records a reject, never a repair

beats.role_note: THE ACTUAL-CODE LAW — the ingest script's own load-bearing rule, verbatim. This is where the episode title comes from.
beats.narration_text: It does not. No recount, no dedupe, no drop, no coercion — written down as the contract, not left to habit. Because the defective envelope declares seven records while holding eight, and one file will not parse. Both have to survive the journey. The last line is the whole thesis: an ingest script that cleans data destroys the evidence that cleaning was needed.
beats.new_visual_element: the TRANSPORT, DO NOT REPAIR contract, verbatim

shot.show: the ingest script's TRANSPORT, DO NOT REPAIR docstring block

props.title: scripts/ingest/...-ingest-inputs.py
props.code:
TRANSPORT, DO NOT REPAIR -- the load-bearing rule of this step:
    This script carries source payloads into the raw layer verbatim.
    It does NOT recount records, drop malformed rows, fill missing
    fields, coerce types, or dedupe.

      - D12: the envelope declares record_count 7 while holding 8 rows.
        Were ingest to "helpfully" recount, step 3's record_count check
        would have nothing left to catch.

      - D18: the .broken file does not parse. This step neither raises
        nor silently skips it; it copies the bytes through unchanged.

    An ingest script that cleans data destroys the evidence that
    cleaning was needed.

beats.role_note: cycle 1 output — step 2 scored on the three axes. MOVING, never a still.
beats.narration_text: Score it. Decides: nothing about content. Refuses: every repair it could obviously make. Evidence: an envelope reporting exactly what it moved, with the source's own declared count preserved beside it. That is a stage doing one job. The discipline is in the refusal, not the transport.
beats.new_visual_element: step 2 scored on DECIDES / REFUSES / EVIDENCE

shot.show: the three axis rows with step 2's answers filled in
shot.visual_intent: The three framework rows return as headers. Step 2's column fills cell by cell as each is named — nothing / every repair / the envelope. The REFUSES cell lands in terracotta, because that is the load-bearing one.

beats.role_note: THE REVISION LAW — cycle 2, the opposite job
beats.narration_text: Step three is the opposite job. This one does judge. But only shape: required fields, rows that parse, and whether the declared count is honest.

shot.show: the Claude composer carrying the step-3 prompt

props.command: claude "write step 3: validate shape against the manifest contract, promote only clean rows to data/verified/, and catch only the defects step 3 owns"
output: required fields · parseable rows · honest count

beats.role_note: THE ACTUAL-CODE LAW — the SCOPE block, verbatim; the refusal is written into the file
beats.narration_text: And its scope is written into the file. Against the frozen corpus it must surface exactly eight of the eighteen catalogued defects, named by id. The other ten — duplicates, stale timestamps, type violations — belong to step four and are deliberately not detected here. The comment gives the reason: catching them early would make step four untestable.

props.title: scripts/gigo/...-validate-data-shape.py
props.code:
SCOPE -- what this step is responsible for catching:
    This step owns shape only. Against the frozen corpus it must
    surface exactly 8 of the 18 catalogued defects:

      missing_fields : D01, D07, D08, D14
      parse_errors   : D09, D15, D18
      record_count   : D12

    The other 10 -- duplicates, stale timestamps, type violations --
    belong to step 4 and are deliberately NOT detected here.
    Catching them early would make step 4 untestable.
props.sparkLine: Scope is a contract, not a habit

beats.role_note: cycle 2 output — the live run, real counts. Includes the honest contract gap.
beats.narration_text: Run it. Clean set: nothing found, exit zero. Defective set: four missing required fields, three parse errors, one count mismatch. Eight findings, then a hard stop with exit one — it reports everything before it halts, so one early rejection cannot hide the rest. And there is one field I like: types deferred to step four. A wrong-typed value has no output field in the recipe's contract, so instead of smuggling it into missing fields, the step records the gap and leaves it alone.
beats.new_visual_element: the live run — 8 findings, split by kind, and the deferred gap

shot.show: clean run exit 0 beside defective run exit 1 with 4 / 3 / 1 findings, and the deferred field
shot.visual_intent: Two run panels side by side, held: CLEAN (0 findings, exit 0) and DEFECTIVE (4 missing, 3 parse, 1 count = 8, exit 1). Beneath, the deferred line in terracotta: 10 defects belong to step 4, and types have no field at all.

beats.role_note: PROOF rubric — the failure the framework PREDICTS from axis 3 (EVIDENCE). Real bug from this commit.
beats.narration_text: Now the one that nearly broke everything, and axis three predicted it. This pipeline hashes file bytes to build a provenance trace an auditor can re-verify. But git was checking out C R L F on Windows. So the same file had a different hash depending on which machine cloned it. Evidence that changes with the platform is not evidence. Two fixes: a scoped git attributes pinning these paths to L F, and every write site passing newline backslash n, because write text was translating on the way out too.
beats.new_visual_element: one file, two platforms, two different hashes

shot.show: the same file hashing differently on two platforms, side by side, then pinned to one
shot.visual_intent: One file icon splits into two paths — Linux LF and Windows CRLF — each resolving to a DIFFERENT sha256 prefix, held side by side. Terracotta verdict: a hash that changes with the platform is not evidence. Then both collapse back to one hash as the eol=lf pin lands.

beats.role_note: the ledger moves — what closed, what is still open, stated plainly
beats.narration_text: So the ledger moves. The run envelope exists, so gate two clears. Data verified exists, so gate three clears. Three of six steps are written. Still open: three steps, and the type-violation gap, logged rather than fixed. Reruns are byte-identical, which is the part I will keep testing.
beats.new_visual_element: the week's ledger — closed versus still open

shot.show: two-column ledger: closed this week versus still open, with the commit named
shot.visual_intent: Left column fills in ink: gate 2 clears, gate 3 clears, 3 of 6 steps, reruns byte-identical. Right column stays terracotta: 3 steps unwritten, type-violation gap logged not fixed. Kicker names commit bdc1bc1.

beats.role_note: HANDOFF LAW + PROOF active-task rule — scaffold with good/bad discriminator, read aloud
beats.narration_text: Your turn, and it is question two. Take one stage of a pipeline you own and ask what it could fix that it should not. Paste this. List everything this function silently repairs, and for each one, name the downstream check that would then never fire. A good answer names a real repair and the test it hides. A bad answer tells you the function looks fine.
beats.new_visual_element: Claude composer, the handoff prompt typed in

shot.show: the Claude composer with the viewer's prompt and the good/bad test

props.command: claude "list everything this function silently repairs — coercions, defaults, dedupes, drops. For each, name the downstream check that would then never fire."
output: GOOD: a real repair + the test it hides
a helpful stage is a deleted test
